items.name: scroll-area
items.title: Scroll Area
items.description: A scrolling region with thin, themed scrollbars that look the same on every platform. Native scrolling underneath.

meta.when: A bounded list or panel inside a surface: a menu, a sidebar, a log. Give it a height (or a max height). The page itself, and anything that can simply grow, should scroll natively.
meta.example:
Long content…
…

items.name: scrubber
items.title: Scrubber
items.description: The time bar of a player: a slider over the length of a clip that shows what has played and what has loaded, marks chapters, and can show the time and a picture for the moment under the pointer.

meta.when: Seeking in audio, video or any timeline measured in seconds. video-player and audio-player already contain one bound to their media; use this directly for a custom player or a timeline. For choosing a number that is not a time use slider. Time runs left to right in every language (as on players everywhere: the bar is a picture of time, like a clock face, not a line of text), so the bar and its arrow keys are not mirrored in right-to-left pages; pass `dir="rtl"` if a product decides otherwise, and the keys follow what is drawn.

items.name: segmented-control
items.title: Segmented Control
items.description: A row of two to five segments where exactly one is chosen, with a marker that slides to the choice.

meta.when: Switching one setting between a few short, equal options that take effect at once: a view (list or map), a unit, a period (day, week, month). It is a radio group, so one option is always chosen. For switching panels of content use tabs; for options that can each be on or off use toggle-group or chip; for more than five options use select.
meta.example:
<SegmentedControl defaultValue="list" aria-label="View">
  <SegmentedControlItem value="list">List</SegmentedControlItem>
  <SegmentedControlItem value="map">Map</SegmentedControlItem>
</SegmentedControl>

// Controlled, full width, with icons
<SegmentedControl value={period} onValueChange={setPeriod} aria-label="Period" className="w-full">
  <SegmentedControlItem value="day"><Sun /> Day</SegmentedControlItem>
  <SegmentedControlItem value="week"><Calendar /> Week</SegmentedControlItem>
</SegmentedControl>

items.name: select
items.title: Select
items.description: A themed dropdown for choosing one value from a list, with groups, labels and separators. Never a native select.

meta.when: Picking one of more than about five options, or when space is tight. For two to five visible options use radio-group; for a short row of icons use toggle-group.
meta.example:
<Select defaultValue="eur">
  <SelectTrigger aria-label="Currency" className="w-48">
    <SelectValue placeholder="Currency" />
  </SelectTrigger>
  <SelectContent>
    <SelectGroup>
      <SelectLabel>Europe</SelectLabel>
      <SelectItem value="eur">Euro</SelectItem>
      <SelectItem value="sek">Swedish krona</SelectItem>
    </SelectGroup>
    <SelectSeparator />
    <SelectGroup>
      <SelectLabel>Americas</SelectLabel>
      <SelectItem value="usd">US dollar</SelectItem>
      <SelectItem value="cad" disabled>Canadian dollar</SelectItem>
    </SelectGroup>
  </SelectContent>
</Select>

items.name: separator
items.title: Separator
items.description: A hairline between two pieces of content, horizontal or vertical, with an optional label in the middle.

meta.when: Dividing groups inside a surface or a toolbar. Between page sections use section spacing instead, and inside a list prefer a border on the rows.
meta.example:
or continue with
Docs Blog

items.name: sheet
items.title: Sheet
items.description: A modal panel that slides in from an edge of the screen, with parts for a header, title, description and footer.

meta.when: Navigation, filters, details or a longer form beside the page. `side` is "end" by default ("start" and "end" follow the reading direction; "left" and "right" do not); on phones "bottom" is the natural choice, because it is within reach of the thumb. For a short decision in the middle of the screen use dialog. Always give it a SheetTitle (add className="sr-only" to hide it). Opened by state with no SheetTrigger, focus does not return on close: remember the opener (`opener.current = document.activeElement`) and refocus it in `onCloseAutoFocus={(event) => { event.preventDefault(); opener.current?.focus(); }}` on SheetContent.
meta.example:
Filters Narrow the list of projects.
…

items.name: skeleton
items.title: Skeleton
items.description: A pulsing block that stands in for content that is loading: a bare block sized by hand, lines of text, or a wrapper that takes the exact size of the real content. It is still under reduced motion.

meta.when: Content whose shape is known is on its way. Nothing may jump when it arrives: either size the block like the thing it replaces, or wrap the real component (rendered with placeholder data) in `<Skeleton loading>` so the box is exactly its final size. Mark the region that is loading with `aria-busy="true"`: the placeholders themselves are hidden from assistive technology. For an unknown wait use spinner; for a measurable one use progress.
meta.example: // Holds the final size: the card is laid out, invisible and inert, under the placeholder

items.name: slider
items.title: Slider
items.description: A slider for one value, or a range with two thumbs.

meta.when: Choosing a number where the rough position matters more than the exact figure: volume, a price range. When the exact number matters use an input with type="number".
meta.example:
<Slider defaultValue={[40]} max={100} step={5} aria-label="Volume" />
<Slider defaultValue={[200, 800]} min={0} max={1000} step={50} thumbLabels={["Lowest price", "Highest price"]} />

items.name: slot-picker
items.title: Slot Picker
items.description: Offered times as a set of pills to choose one from, optionally under named groups, each able to carry a note and to be unavailable for a stated reason.

meta.when: The times are a short list that someone else decides: appointment slots, sittings, departures. One is chosen, so it is a radio group. For any time of the person's own choosing use time-picker; for more than about twenty slots, narrow them first (by day, by part of the day) or use select.
meta.example:
<SlotPicker defaultValue="10:00" aria-label="Time" locale="en-GB">
  <SlotPickerGroup label="Morning">
    <SlotPickerItem value="09:30" />
    <SlotPickerItem value="10:00" note="2 places left" />
    <SlotPickerItem value="11:30" unavailable="Full" />
  </SlotPickerGroup>
  <SlotPickerGroup label="Afternoon">
    <SlotPickerItem value="14:00" />
  </SlotPickerGroup>
</SlotPicker>

// Controlled, with its own labels, and nothing on offer
<SlotPicker value={slot} onValueChange={setSlot} aria-label="Sitting">
  {sittings.length === 0 ? <SlotPickerEmpty>Nothing is open on this day.</SlotPickerEmpty> : null}
  {sittings.map((sitting) => <SlotPickerItem key={sitting.id} value={sitting.id}>{sitting.name}</SlotPickerItem>)}
</SlotPicker>

items.name: sortable-list
items.title: Sortable List
items.description: A list whose order the person sets, three ways: dragging a row by its handle (mouse, pen or touch), lifting it with the keyboard and moving it with the arrow keys, or pressing "Move up" and "Move down" buttons. Every move is read out.

meta.when: The order itself is the data: the stops of a plan, priorities, pictures in a gallery, columns to show. Always give the rows SortableMoveButtons or a SortableHandle (both is best): dragging alone leaves out people who cannot drag (WCAG 2.5.7). It is one vertical list; it does not move rows between lists or sort a grid. For a list sorted by a rule (newest first) use a select for the rule instead; for choosing rather than ordering use chip or checkboxes.

items.name: spinner
items.title: Spinner
items.description: A turning ring that says something is in progress, announced to assistive technology by its label.

meta.when: A short wait of unknown length. Inside a button use the button's `loading` prop; when the shape of the content is known use skeleton; when the amount done is known use progress.
meta.example: Saving

items.name: stat
items.title: Stat
items.description: A number tile: a label, a value, an optional change with its direction, and a slot for a sparkline.

meta.when: A headline figure on a dashboard or in a bento cell. Pass `change` as a magnitude ("12%"): the sign and the arrow are added from `direction`. For several figures compared over time use a chart or a table.
meta.example:
<Stat label="Revenue" value="€48,200" change="12%" direction="up" changeLabel="vs last month" />
<Stat label="Churn" value="2.1%" change="0.4 pts" direction="up" tone="negative" />
<Stat
  label="Uptime"
  value="99.98%"
  chart={
    <svg viewBox="0 0 100 24" preserveAspectRatio="none" className="h-8 w-full" aria-hidden="true">
      <polyline points="0,18 20,14 40,16 60,8 80,10 100,4" fill="none" strokeWidth="1.5" className="stroke-chart-1" />
    </svg>
  }
/>

items.name: status-line
items.title: Status Line
items.description: One line that says in words what is happening now ("Searching", "Writing a reply", "Done"), read out politely by screen readers, with an optional moving mark and a slot for a stop button.

meta.when: Beside a thread or any surface where work goes on that the person waits for: it is the one polite live region of that surface. Render it from the start, empty, and change its text: a region that appears together with its text is often not announced. It keeps its height when empty, so nothing jumps. For a wait with no words use spinner; for a measurable one use progress; for a result that must outlive the moment use alert or toaster.
meta.example:
<StatusLine working={busy} action={busy ? <StatusLineAction onClick={stop}>Stop</StatusLineAction> : null}>
  {busy ? "Searching three sources" : ""}
</StatusLine>

items.name: steps
items.title: Steps
items.description: A rail that shows where one is in a sequence of steps: a row of thin segments, or numbered markers with titles, each step with a state (done, filled in for you, current, not started, skipped, blocked).

meta.when: Showing progress through a known, ordered set of steps: a booking, a sign-up, an import, a checklist that runs in order. Use "segments" above a card where space is short and "labelled" where the step names help. Pair it with StepsCount ("Step 2 of 5"), which says the same in words. For a measured amount of one task use progress; for the whole guided task with its buttons use wizard, which draws this rail itself; for moving between unordered views use tabs.
meta.example:
<StepsCount current={2} total={4} />
<Steps aria-label="Booking progress">
  <Step state="done">Dates</Step>
  <Step state="current">People</Step>
  <Step state="upcoming">Extras</Step>
  <Step state="upcoming">Review</Step>
</Steps>

// Numbered markers with titles; a finished step can be a button that goes back to it
<Steps variant="labelled" aria-label="Import">
  <Step state="done" onClick={() => goTo("file")}>Choose a file</Step>
  <Step state="assumed" note="Taken from the file's first row">Match the columns</Step>
  <Step state="current" description="About a minute">Check the rows</Step>
  <Step state="skipped">Add notes</Step>
</Steps>

items.name: streaming-text
items.title: Streaming Text
items.description: Text that grows as it arrives, with a caret while it is arriving, that is never read out word by word: it is announced once, when it is finished.

meta.when: A reply from a model, a transcript or a log line that streams in. Pass the text so far and whether more is coming. It must not sit inside a live region (a thread is `aria-live="off"`); say "Writing a reply" through a status-line while it streams. For text that is already complete use a plain element; for a headline that animates in use text-reveal.
meta.example:
<MessageContent>
  <StreamingText text={reply} streaming={isStreaming} announceWhenDone onDone={saveReply} />
</MessageContent>

// A shorter spoken form, and words that fade in as they land
<StreamingText text={reply} streaming={isStreaming} reveal="word" announceWhenDone="Three places found. The nearest is ten minutes away." />

// The project's own renderer (Markdown, for example)
<StreamingText text={reply} streaming={isStreaming}>{(text) => <Markdown>{text}</Markdown>}</StreamingText>

items.name: switch
items.title: Switch
items.description: An on/off switch.

meta.when: A setting that takes effect as soon as it is flipped. For a choice that is submitted with a form use checkbox; for a pressed/unpressed toolbar button use toggle.
meta.example:
<Label><Switch defaultChecked /> Weekly summary</Label>
<Switch aria-label="Dark mode" checked={dark} onCheckedChange={setDark} />

items.name: table
items.title: Table
items.description: A semantic table with styled parts, inside a wrapper that scrolls sideways so it never overflows a narrow screen.

meta.when: Rows of the same kind of thing compared across columns. For sorting, filtering and paging build on these parts. For two or three facts per item use cards; for one number use stat.
meta.example: Invoices this quarter Invoice Status Amount INV-001 Paid €250.00 Total €250.00

items.name: tabs
items.title: Tabs
items.description: Panels that share one place, switched by a row of tabs. Two looks: an underline, or a segmented pill.

meta.when: Views of the same thing that people switch between without leaving the page. `variant="underline"` (the default) for sections of a page; `variant="pill"` for a compact switch between two to four views. For moving between pages use links (navbar, breadcrumb); for stacked sections that can be open together use accordion.
meta.example:
<Tabs defaultValue="overview">
  <TabsList aria-label="Project">
    <TabsTrigger value="overview">Overview</TabsTrigger>
    <TabsTrigger value="activity">Activity</TabsTrigger>
  </TabsList>
  <TabsContent value="overview">The overview.</TabsContent>
  <TabsContent value="activity">The activity.</TabsContent>
</Tabs>

<Tabs defaultValue="month">
  <TabsList variant="pill" aria-label="Billing period">
    <TabsTrigger value="month">Monthly</TabsTrigger>
    <TabsTrigger value="year">Yearly</TabsTrigger>
  </TabsList>
  <TabsContent value="month">Billed every month.</TabsContent>
  <TabsContent value="year">Billed once a year.</TabsContent>
</Tabs>

items.name: textarea
items.title: Textarea
items.description: A multi-line text input that grows with its content, with an invalid state.

meta.when: Free text of more than one line: a message, a note, a description. Wrap it in field for a label and an error; use input for a single line.
meta.example:
<Textarea placeholder="Tell us about the project" rows={4} />
<Textarea aria-invalid="true" aria-label="Message" defaultValue="Too short" />

items.name: theme-provider
items.title: Theme Provider
items.description: Holds the theme (light or dark, roundness, highlight colour), applies it to the page, remembers the visitor's choice, and avoids a flash of the wrong theme.

meta.when: Once, around the app in the root layout, when visitors or the product can change the theme. For a fixed theme, skip it and set the attributes on <html> by hand.

items.name: thread
items.title: Thread
items.description: The scrolling log of a conversation: it follows the newest content while the person is at the bottom, stops the moment they scroll up, and offers a way back down.

meta.when: A conversation with an assistant or between people, where messages arrive over time. It holds no messages and no transport: render them inside it (message, streaming-text, part-frame). The log is deliberately silent (`aria-live="off"`): say what is happening through one status-line beside it, and the finished reply once through streaming-text's `announceWhenDone`. For a list that does not grow at the bottom use scroll-area.
meta.example:
<Thread aria-label="Conversation with the assistant" className="h-[32rem]">
  <ThreadContent>
    {messages.length === 0 ? <ThreadEmpty>Ask anything to begin.</ThreadEmpty> : null}
    {messages.map((message) => (
      <ThreadTurn key={message.id} label={message.from === "user" ? "You" : "Assistant"}>
        <Message from={message.from}>
          <MessageBody><MessageContent>{message.text}</MessageContent></MessageBody>
        </Message>
      </ThreadTurn>
    ))}
  </ThreadContent>
  <ThreadJump>Jump to latest</ThreadJump>
</Thread>

// Always show what the person just sent, even if they had scrolled up
<Thread aria-label="Conversation" resumeKey={lastOwnMessageId}>…</Thread>

items.name: tile-group
items.title: Tile Group
items.description: A grid of large tiles, each a picture or an icon with a word, where one or several are chosen.

meta.when: A choice that is easier to make by looking than by reading: moods, styles, room types, plans. Each tile must carry a visible word; the picture alone is never the label. For short text-only options use chip (ChipGroup); for a compact switch between a few views use segmented-control; for a long list use select or combobox.
meta.example: Quiet Gardens, reading rooms, slow walks Lively

items.name: time-picker
items.title: Time Picker
items.description: A time field made of an hour and a minute that are each stepped with the arrow keys or typed, with an AM/PM part where the locale uses a 12-hour clock. The value is a 24-hour "HH:mm" string.

meta.when: Any time of the person's own choosing: an opening hour, a reminder, an arrival. When the times on offer are a fixed list use slot-picker. Never the browser's native time input. Name it with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.
meta.example:
Opens at

// Controlled, limited, 12-hour whatever the locale, with translated names

items.name: timeline
items.title: Timeline
items.description: An ordered list of numbered rows joined by a line: each with an optional time, a title and content, and a state (done, current, upcoming).

meta.when: Things that happen in an order: the parts of a day, the stages of an order or a delivery, a history of changes, the steps of a plan. The number and the state are read out with each row. For the steps of a form the person is filling in use steps; for rows people reorder use sortable-list; for unordered items use a plain list.
meta.example:
<Timeline aria-label="Saturday">
  <TimelineItem state="done">
    <TimelineTime dateTime="2026-03-14T09:30">09:30</TimelineTime>
    <TimelineTitle>Market walk</TimelineTitle>
    <TimelineContent>Meet at the north gate.</TimelineContent>
  </TimelineItem>
  <TimelineItem state="current">
    <TimelineTime dateTime="2026-03-14T12:30">12:30</TimelineTime>
    <TimelineTitle>Lunch</TimelineTitle>
  </TimelineItem>
  <TimelineItem>
    <TimelineTitle>Free afternoon</TimelineTitle>
  </TimelineItem>
</Timeline>

items.name: toaster
items.title: Toaster
items.description: The place where toasts appear: sonner's Toaster drawn with the theme's tokens, and its `toast` function.

meta.when: Short confirmations and errors that need no decision ("Saved", "Could not connect"). Render one Toaster in the root layout, then call `toast` from anywhere on the client. For something that must be answered use dialog; for a message that belongs to a field or a section, show it there.

items.name: toggle-group
items.title: Toggle Group
items.description: A joined row of toggles where one (type="single") or several (type="multiple") are on.

meta.when: A compact choice between a few short options or icons: alignment, a view switcher, text styles. For options with longer labels use radio-group (one) or checkboxes (several); for switching panels use tabs.
meta.example:
<ToggleGroup type="single" defaultValue="grid" aria-label="View" variant="outline">
  <ToggleGroupItem value="grid">Grid</ToggleGroupItem>
  <ToggleGroupItem value="list">List</ToggleGroupItem>
</ToggleGroup>
<ToggleGroup type="multiple" aria-label="Text style" size="sm">
  <ToggleGroupItem value="italic" aria-label="Italic"><Italic strokeWidth={1.5} /></ToggleGroupItem>
  <ToggleGroupItem value="underline" aria-label="Underline"><Underline strokeWidth={1.5} /></ToggleGroupItem>
</ToggleGroup>

items.name: toggle
items.title: Toggle
items.description: A button that stays pressed: on or off.

meta.when: A toolbar state such as bold, mute or pin. For a setting use switch; for several toggles that belong together, or a pick-one row, use toggle-group.
meta.example:
<Toggle aria-label="Italic"><Italic strokeWidth={1.5} /></Toggle>
<Toggle variant="outline" size="sm" defaultPressed>Pinned</Toggle>

items.name: tooltip
items.title: Tooltip
items.description: A few words that appear beside a control on hover or keyboard focus.

meta.when: Naming an icon-only button or adding a short hint. It does not open on touch, so never put anything needed there: the control keeps its own `aria-label`. For content people interact with use popover. Put one TooltipProvider around the app (root layout); every Tooltip must be inside one.
meta.example:
<TooltipProvider>
  <Tooltip>
    <TooltipTrigger asChild>
      <Button variant="ghost" size="icon" aria-label="Copy link"><Link2 /></Button>
    </TooltipTrigger>
    <TooltipContent>Copy link</TooltipContent>
  </Tooltip>
</TooltipProvider>

items.name: undo-line
items.title: Undo Line
items.description: A line that stays where something was just done, says what it was, and offers to undo it.

meta.when: After an action that can be taken back, inside the place it happened: a row removed from a plan, a message archived, a change applied by an assistant. It stays until it is dismissed or the next action replaces it, so it is not missed the way a toast is by someone using a screen reader, a magnifier or a slow hand. For news that needs no answer and is unrelated to one place use toaster; for a decision before the action use dialog.
meta.example:
{removed ? (
  <UndoLine>
    <UndoLineMessage>Lunch was removed from Saturday.</UndoLineMessage>
    <UndoLineAction onClick={restore}>Undo</UndoLineAction>
    <UndoLineDismiss aria-label="Dismiss" onClick={() => setRemoved(null)} />
  </UndoLine>
) : null}

items.name: video-player
items.title: Video Player
items.description: The parts of a video player around a `<video>` element the project renders: a frame that keeps its shape, controls that step back while it plays, play, mute, volume, time, a scrubber, captions, speed, full screen, and words for loading and failure.

meta.when: Any video a person controls: a clip on a page, a lesson, a recording. The project gives the element its sources (a file, or HLS attached to the element); the parts only drive it, so compose the ones the clip needs. Nothing plays by itself: for a silent, looping decoration use a plain `<video muted loop>` with its own pause control. For sound alone use audio-player; for a picture viewer use lightbox.
meta.example:
<VideoPlayer aria-label="How the kiln is loaded" defaultCaptions>
  <VideoPlayerVideo src="/kiln.mp4" poster="/kiln.jpg">
    <track kind="captions" src="/kiln.en.vtt" srcLang="en" label="English" />
  </VideoPlayerVideo>
  <VideoPlayerLoading />
  <VideoPlayerError />
  <Captions />
  <VideoPlayerControls>
    <VideoPlayerScrubber />
    <VideoPlayerControlsRow>
      <VideoPlayerPlay />
      <VideoPlayerMute />
      <VideoPlayerVolume />
      <VideoPlayerTime />
      <VideoPlayerCaptionsButton className="ms-auto" />
      <VideoPlayerRate />
      <VideoPlayerFullscreen />
    </VideoPlayerControlsRow>
  </VideoPlayerControls>
</VideoPlayer>

items.name: virtual-list
items.title: Virtual List
items.description: A long list or grid that renders only the rows in view: thousands of items of any height in a box that scrolls, or down a page that scrolls with the window, each still announced with its position in the whole list, with a way to go to an item and to come back to where the person was.

meta.when: More items than the page should hold at once (a few hundred or more): a feed, a log, search results, a picture library. Rows may have any height: each is measured once it is drawn and the rest are estimated, and the view does not jump when a row above it turns out taller. Give the box a height and a name (`aria-label`); or, where the list is the page (a feed, results under a header), `scroll="window"` and no height: it then grows to its full length and the window scrolls it. For a short list render the rows plainly; for a conversation that grows at the bottom use thread; for pages of results use pagination. Written here on ResizeObserver instead of adding a virtualisation package: a headless one would bring the offsets but not the roles, the positions for screen readers, the kept focus or the restoration, which are most of this file.

items.name: wizard
items.title: Wizard
items.description: The shell of a guided task done one step at a time inside a card: a title with "Step 2 of 5", a rail of the steps, the current step, and Back, Skip and a main button named after what the step does.

meta.when: A task that is easier one question at a time and has a known order: a booking, a set-up, an application. It keeps where one is (controlled or not), moves focus to each new step's heading, and blocks the main button with a stated reason while a step is not answered. Where a server decides what comes next, control it: give `step`, and `onNext`, `onBack` and `onSkip` in place of the wizard's own moves, with `pending` while the answer is on its way; the step still slides in and its heading still takes focus when `step` changes. For a short form show all the fields at once (field); for the rail alone use steps; for unordered sections use tabs or accordion. What each step contains is yours: the wizard holds no answers.

items.name: aspect
items.title: Aspect
items.description: Holds its content at a fixed width-to-height ratio, so space is reserved before an image, video or canvas loads.

meta.when: Media whose size is not known until it loads, or a tile that must keep its shape at any width. Make the child fill it (`size-full object-cover`). For plain CSS needs the `aspect-video` utility is enough.

items.name: bento-grid
items.title: Bento Grid
items.description: A grid of flat cards of unequal sizes. One column on a phone, two on a tablet, then 2, 3, 4 or 6: decided by the grid's own width, so it works inside any container.

meta.when: Showing several features, figures or pieces of media as one composed block. Cells take `span` and `rowSpan`; spans are clamped to the columns there are. For equal cards use grid; for a single surface use card.
meta.example: // Feature block: one wide lead cell, two small ones, a full-width strip. Themable from one place Light or dark, square to round, any highlight colour. Accessible Fast Yours to edit // Dashboard: four figures on top, a wide chart beside a tall list. …chart… …recent activity… // Link mosaic: six columns, mixed sizes, gaps back-filled, every cell a link. … … … … …

items.name: container
items.title: Container
items.description: Centres content at the page width with the page gutter on both sides. Four sizes: narrow, page, wide, full.

meta.when: Around the content of every page band so edges line up down the page. "narrow" for reading text, "wide" for galleries and dashboards, "full" to keep only the gutter. Section already wraps its children in one.
meta.example:
Pricing
Long-form text…

items.name: grid
items.title: Grid
items.description: A responsive grid of equal columns that fits as many as the width allows, from a minimum column width. No breakpoints.

meta.when: A set of like items: cards, logos, stats, thumbnails. It reflows inside any width, including a sidebar. For tiles of different sizes use bento-grid; for two fixed columns use split.
meta.example:
<Grid min="16rem" gap="md">
  <Card>…</Card>
  <Card>…</Card>
  <Card>…</Card>
</Grid>
<Grid min="9rem" gap="sm" fit="fill">{logos}</Grid>

items.name: map-frame
items.title: Map Frame
items.description: The frame around a map, not a map: it holds the map's size, shows a still until the person asks for the map, keeps a text list beside it, and takes the map to full screen and back. The map engine is yours.

meta.when: Any page that shows a map from any engine (MapLibre, Leaflet, a hosted maps script). It gives the map what an engine does not: no request to a third party before the person presses the button (put the line about that in MapFrameNotice), no layout shift, the same information as a list (MapFrameList) so that the map is never the only way to it, a way to skip past the map with the keyboard, and full screen that behaves as a modal. For a still picture of a place with no interaction use an image in aspect.
meta.example:
Show the map The map is loaded from Example Maps, which will see your address.

  1. {stop.name}, {stop.address}
    2. )}

items.name: marquee
items.title: Marquee
items.description: A row that scrolls sideways without end. It pauses on hover and on keyboard focus, and under reduced motion it is an ordinary wrapped row.

meta.when: A strip of logos, short quotes or tags where no single item must be read. Not for content the reader needs: everything is also in the markup once, but it moves. For a few items that fit, use stack or grid.
meta.example: Design Build Launch

items.name: section
items.title: Section
items.description: A band of a page with consistent vertical rhythm, an optional eyebrow, title and description, and three tones: default, muted, inverse.

meta.when: Every top-level block of a marketing or content page. "inverse" makes a dark band on a light page and re-themes everything inside it. Inside an app screen use stack and card instead.
meta.example:
<Section eyebrow="Features" title="Everything in one place" description="Built on the same tokens.">
  <BentoGrid>…</BentoGrid>
</Section>
<Section tone="inverse" align="center" title="Ready to start?">
  <Button>Get in touch</Button>
</Section>
<Section tone="muted" spacing="sm" container="narrow">Plain content, no header.</Section>

items.name: split
items.title: Split
items.description: Two columns, usually media beside text, that stack into one on a narrow width. A ratio between the columns and a reverse option.

meta.when: A feature row, a hero with an image, a form beside its explanation. Give it exactly two children. Alternate `reverse` down a page for a zigzag. For more than two columns use grid.
meta.example:
See everything at once

One screen for the whole week.

 … …

items.name: stack
items.title: Stack
items.description: A flex row or column with a gap from a fixed scale, and props for alignment, distribution and wrapping.

meta.when: Spacing a run of siblings evenly: form fields, a button row, a header with actions. For columns that reflow by width use grid; for unequal tiles use bento-grid.
meta.example:
Title

Body

  • One
  • Two

items.name: film-stage
items.title: Film Stage
items.description: A stage for a sequence of timed scenes with a transport: it owns the clock and the chrome (play, time bar, speed, sound), mounts the scene for the current moment, cuts or crossfades between scenes, and can draw any moment on request for export.

meta.when: Content the project draws itself from a time: an animated explainer, a story in scenes, a slideshow with narration, a film assembled from markup, SVG or canvas. Each scene gets its own local time and draws from it, so any frame can be drawn again exactly. The stage is the clock other things follow: scrubber, scene-strip, captions and hotspots work inside it as they do inside video-player, and any number of sounds (a clip for each narrated line, a bed under them) are kept in step, each from its own start for its own length. For a video or sound file use video-player or audio-player; for motion tied to scrolling use scroll-scene; for a set of pictures a person pages through use carousel.
meta.example:

items.name: layout-transition
items.title: Layout Transition
items.description: A shared element that animates from one place to another: render Morph with the same layoutId in two places and it travels between them.

meta.when: A tabs or navigation indicator that slides to the active item, a card that grows into its detail view, a selection highlight. Both places must be in the same React tree. Between pages use view-transition; for content that only appears and disappears use presence.

items.name: magnetic
items.title: Magnetic
items.description: A wrapper whose child is gently pulled toward the pointer while it is hovered, and springs back when the pointer leaves.

meta.when: The one main call to action on a marketing page, or an icon button that should feel alive. Not for every button, not inside dense interfaces, and it does nothing on touch screens.
meta.example:
<Magnetic>
  <Button size="lg">Start a project</Button>
</Magnetic>
<Magnetic strength={0.5}>
  <Button variant="outline" size="icon" aria-label="Play"><Play /></Button>
</Magnetic>

items.name: number-ticker
items.title: Number Ticker
items.description: A number that counts up to its value when it scrolls into view, formatted with Intl.NumberFormat.

meta.when: A headline statistic: customers, revenue, a percentage. Not for values that update live (render those directly), and not for more than a few on one screen.
meta.example:
<NumberTicker value={12480} />
<NumberTicker value={0.9997} options={{ style: "percent", maximumFractionDigits: 2 }} />
<NumberTicker value={48000} locale="de-DE" options={{ style: "currency", currency: "EUR", maximumFractionDigits: 0 }} />

items.name: page-transition
items.title: Page Transition
items.description: Wraps page content and plays a short enter (a fade and a small rise) each time the route changes.

meta.when: The content area of an app or site, once, in the layout. The first page load is not animated. Where the browser supports it and elements should morph between pages, use view-transition instead; do not use both.

items.name: parallax
items.title: Parallax
items.description: A clipped frame whose layer moves at a different speed from the page as it scrolls past.

meta.when: A background image or a decorative layer behind a section. The frame needs a height of its own (an aspect ratio or a fixed height). Not for text that must be read while it moves; for a pinned, scroll-told sequence use scroll-scene.

items.name: presence
items.title: Presence
items.description: Animates its children in when they are shown and out before they are removed.

meta.when: Conditional UI that is not a Radix primitive: an inline notice, a revealed panel, a step that swaps. Radix dialogs, popovers and menus already animate with their own classes; for content entering on scroll use reveal.
meta.example:
const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
<Button onClick={() => setOpen((value) => !value)}>Toggle</Button>
<Presence show={open} preset="slide-up" className="mt-4 rounded-surface border p-4">
  Saved. Your changes are live.
</Presence>

items.name: reveal
items.title: Reveal
items.description: Fades and moves its content into place when it scrolls into view.

meta.when: A section, card or image that should arrive as the page is read. For a list revealed one after another use stagger; for a heading use text-reveal; for conditional UI that mounts and unmounts use presence.
meta.example: Built to be owned

items.name: scroll-progress
items.title: Scroll Progress
items.description: A thin bar fixed to the top of the viewport that fills as the page, or one element, is scrolled through.

meta.when: Long reading pages: an article, documentation, a case study. Pass `target` to follow the article rather than the whole page. Not a loading indicator (use a progress control for that).

<ScrollProgress target={article} className="h-1" />
<article ref={article}>…</article>

meta.when: A product story told as the visitor scrolls: steps that replace each other, a device that turns, a diagram that builds. Use sparingly, one or two per page. For a simple entrance use reveal; for a drifting background use parallax.

items.name: spotlight
items.title: Spotlight
items.description: A surface on which a soft light in the highlight colour follows the pointer.

meta.when: A hero panel, a feature card or a call-to-action band that should respond to the pointer. Give it a border and a background like any surface. Decoration only: it does nothing on touch screens, so never rely on it to show something.

items.name: stagger
items.title: Stagger
items.description: A container whose items fade and move into place one after another when it scrolls into view.

meta.when: A grid of cards, a feature list, a row of logos. For one block use reveal; for the words of a heading use text-reveal.
meta.example:
<Stagger className="grid gap-4 sm:grid-cols-3" interval={0.08}>
  <StaggerItem><Card>Design</Card></StaggerItem>

items.name: text-reveal
items.title: Text Reveal
items.description: Reveals a heading word by word, or line by line, when it scrolls into view.

meta.when: A headline or a short statement. Not for paragraphs of body text (use reveal on the block), and not for text that changes while it is shown.
meta.example:
<TextReveal as="h1" className="text-4xl font-medium" playOnLoad>
  Websites, apps and systems that last
</TextReveal>
<TextReveal as="p" by="line" interval={0.12} className="max-w-prose text-xl">
  We design the brand, build the product and stay to run it.
</TextReveal>

items.name: tilt
items.title: Tilt
items.description: A wrapper that tilts its content in 3D toward the pointer on hover and springs back, with an optional glare.

meta.when: A featured card, a product shot, a pricing plan worth lifting off the page. One or a few per view; not for forms or anything read at length, and it does nothing on touch screens.
meta.example:
<Tilt max={8} glare className="max-w-sm">
  <Card>
    <CardHeader>
      <CardTitle>Studio plan</CardTitle>
      <CardDescription>Everything, for one team</CardDescription>
    </CardHeader>
  </Card>
</Tilt>

items.name: view-transition
items.title: View Transition
items.description: View transitions two ways: wrappers over React's own <ViewTransition> (a shared element that morphs between two places, a boundary that cross-fades what changes inside it), and helpers for the browser's API (run an update as a transition, name an element, a link that navigates inside a transition).

meta.when: Moving between pages or between two states of a view, where an element in the old view should become one in the new. Use the React wrappers (SharedElement, TransitionBoundary) when the change is a React transition: a state update inside startTransition, a Suspense boundary revealing, a navigation by a router that uses transitions (Next.js). React then starts the browser's transition itself. Use the browser helpers (startViewTransition, ViewTransitionName, TransitionLink) when nothing in the tree uses React's component: a synchronous update, a router that does not use transitions, an element that stays mounted while the view around it changes. Do not mix the two for one update: React's documentation says not to call document.startViewTransition yourself around an update it is already animating. Both degrade to an instant change where the API is missing, and the theme switches them off under reduced motion. For a shared element that must be interrupted mid-way use layout-transition; for a simple enter on route change use page-transition.

items.name: floating-shapes
items.title: Floating Shapes
items.description: A few simple solids (icosahedron, torus, box, octahedron) floating and turning slowly, flat-shaded or wireframe, coloured from theme variables.

meta.when: An abstract, geometric accent for a hero or a feature section. Use it inside scene. For a single soft object use orb; to show a real object use model-stage.
meta.example:
<Scene aspect={16 / 9}>
  <FloatingShapes />
</Scene>

<Scene aspect={2}>
  <FloatingShapes
    shapes={[
      { kind: "torus", position: [-1.5, 0, 0], color: "--highlight" },
      { kind: "box", position: [1.5, 0.4, -1], size: 0.8, color: "--foreground", wireframe: true },
    ]}
  />
</Scene>

items.name: globe
items.title: Globe
items.description: A dotted globe that turns slowly and can be dragged to spin, with optional highlighted markers by latitude and longitude.

meta.when: Showing reach or places at a glance: offices, regions, where requests come from. Use it inside scene. For exact values per place use a table or bar-chart; the globe is not a chart.
meta.example:
<Scene aspect={1} className="max-w-lg" label="A globe with markers on Amsterdam, Kochi and San Francisco">
  <Globe
    markers={[
      { lat: 52.37, lon: 4.9 },
      { lat: 9.93, lon: 76.27 },
      { lat: 37.77, lon: -122.42 },
    ]}
  />
</Scene>

items.name: model-stage
items.title: Model Stage
items.description: A turntable for any mesh or group: centres and fits it, turns it slowly, and lets the pointer orbit it within limits.

meta.when: Showing one object: a product, a loaded model, a shape of your own. Use it inside scene. For decoration without a subject use orb or floating-shapes.
meta.example:
<Scene aspect={4 / 3} label="A turning torus knot">
  <ModelStage>
    <mesh>
      <torusKnotGeometry args={[1, 0.32, 128, 16]} />
      <meshStandardMaterial flatShading />
    </mesh>
  </ModelStage>
</Scene>

items.name: model-viewer
items.title: Model Viewer
items.description: Shows one 3D model that a person can turn, zoom and reset: a glTF or GLB file, or Gaussian splats (.spz, .ply, .splat, .ksplat, .sog), with a poster and progress while it loads and a still fallback where 3D cannot run.

meta.when: A file to look at from every side: an object, a product, a scanned place. It is a whole viewer, not a part of scene: for your own meshes inside a react-three-fiber canvas use scene with model-stage. Nothing heavy is in this file: three.js is fetched when the viewer comes near the screen, its glTF loader only for glTF, and Spark (`@sparkjsdev/spark`, installed with this item) only when the file is splats. glTF that carries splats in an extension is not read (Spark has no glTF loader); Draco, Meshopt and KTX2 compression need their decoders set in `configureLoader`. Plain wheel and vertical swipes scroll the page: zoom is pinch, Ctrl with the wheel, the keys or the buttons. To compare two models, give two viewers the same `view` and `bounds` inside compare-slider, with `children={null}` and buttons of your own that change the shared view.
meta.example:
<ModelViewer src="/models/vase.glb" alt="A clay vase with a painted belt" poster="/models/vase.jpg" />

// Splats, turning by itself (never under reduced motion), with a hand-off to AR on phones
<ModelViewer
  src="/models/courtyard.spz"
  alt="The courtyard, scanned in 2026"
  autoRotate
  rotation={[180, 0, 0]}
  ar={{ usdz: "/models/courtyard.usdz", glb: "https://example.com/models/courtyard.glb" }}
/>

// Two viewers, one camera
const [view, setView] = useState<ModelView>({ azimuth: 0, polar: 15, zoom: 1 });
const frame = { center: [0, 4, 0], radius: 9 } as const; // one sphere for both, so they keep their sizes and line up
<ModelViewer src="/models/then.glb" alt="As built" view={view} onViewChange={setView} bounds={frame} />
<ModelViewer src="/models/now.glb" alt="Today" view={view} onViewChange={setView} bounds={frame} />

items.name: orb
items.title: Orb
items.description: A softly morphing sphere in the highlight colour, lit at its rim so it reads on light and dark grounds, leaning gently toward the pointer.

meta.when: A calm focal object for a hero or an empty state. Use it inside scene. For many small elements use particle-field; for a product or object of your own use model-stage.
meta.example:
<Scene aspect={1} className="max-w-md">
  <Orb />
</Scene>

<Scene aspect={16 / 9}>
  <Orb color="--chart-2" speed={0.6} distortion={0.5} detail={32} />
</Scene>

items.name: particle-field
items.title: Particle Field
items.description: A field of small round points drifting slowly, with depth that shifts as the pointer moves.

meta.when: A quiet moving ground behind a hero or a section. Use it inside scene and keep text on top readable. For one focal object use orb; for data use the viz components, never particles.
meta.example:
<Scene className="absolute inset-0">
  <ParticleField />
</Scene>

<Scene aspect={2}>
  <ParticleField count={400} color="--foreground" size={0.03} spread={10} />
</Scene>

items.name: scene
items.title: Scene
items.description: The wrapper every 3D component is used inside: a transparent WebGL canvas that mounts late, pauses off screen and falls back to a static block.

meta.when: Around orb, particle-field, floating-shapes, globe, model-stage or your own react-three-fiber content. Give it a size through the parent or `aspect`. For a decorative background that needs no 3D, use a plain token-coloured block.
meta.example: }>

items.name: area-chart
items.title: Area Chart
items.description: A line chart with the space under each line filled flat at low opacity, optionally stacked so the series add up to a total.

meta.when: One series over time whose volume matters, or a few series that add up to a whole (`stacked`). To compare series that cross each other use line-chart: overlapping fills hide one another.
meta.example:
<AreaChart
  label="Storage used per month, by kind"
  data={[
    { month: new Date("2026-01-01"), images: 12, video: 30 },
    { month: new Date("2026-02-01"), images: 18, video: 42 },
    { month: new Date("2026-03-01"), images: 22, video: 61 },
  ]}
  x="month"
  series={[
    { key: "images", label: "Images" },
    { key: "video", label: "Video" },
  ]}
  stacked
/>

items.name: bar-chart
items.title: Bar Chart
items.description: A bar chart, vertical or horizontal, grouped or stacked, always measured from zero, with a tooltip on hover and arrow-key reading.

meta.when: Comparing amounts across categories. Use `orientation="horizontal"` for long names or a ranking, `stacked` when the series add up to a total, `normalize` to compare each category's split as shares of 100 %. For change over many points in time use line-chart; for a single number use a stat, not one bar.
meta.example:
<BarChart
  label="Orders by channel per quarter"
  data={[
    { quarter: "Q1", web: 320, app: 210 },
    { quarter: "Q2", web: 410, app: 290 },
    { quarter: "Q3", web: 380, app: 350 },
  ]}
  x="quarter"
  series={[
    { key: "web", label: "Web" },
    { key: "app", label: "App" },
  ]}
  showValues
/>

items.name: box-plot
items.title: Box Plot
items.description: The spread of a measure in each of several groups side by side: a box from the first to the third quartile, the median across it, whiskers to the furthest values within 1.5 boxes, and the values beyond them as points; or, as a violin, the shape of each spread.

meta.when: Comparing distributions across groups: which is higher, which is wider, which has outliers. For one group's full shape use histogram; for a few exact numbers per group use bar-chart or dot-plot.
meta.example:
<BoxPlot
  label="Response time by region"
  data={[
    { region: "North", ms: 120 }, { region: "North", ms: 140 }, { region: "North", ms: 135 }, { region: "North", ms: 310 },
    { region: "South", ms: 90 }, { region: "South", ms: 110 }, { region: "South", ms: 105 }, { region: "South", ms: 98 },
  ]}
  group="region"
  value="ms"
  valueLabel="Milliseconds"
/>

items.name: calendar-heatmap
items.title: Calendar Heatmap
items.description: A value per day laid out as a calendar, a column for each week and a row for each weekday, coloured on one hue from faint to strong, with month and weekday names and arrow keys that move by day and by week.

meta.when: Showing a daily measure over months: activity, sales per day, rainfall, where the pattern by weekday and season matters. For a few weeks with exact values use bar-chart; for a trend use line-chart; to pick a day use calendar.
meta.example:
<CalendarHeatmap
  label="Workouts per day"
  data={[{ day: "2026-01-05", count: 1 }, { day: "2026-01-06", count: 2 }, { day: "2026-01-09", count: 1 }]}
  day="day"
  value="count"
  from="2026-01-01"
  to="2026-03-31"
/>

items.name: chart
items.title: Chart
items.description: The shared parts every chart is built from: a container that measures itself and carries the text alternative, an SVG root, a tooltip, a legend, series styles, and axis and format helpers.

meta.when: Building a chart of your own that should match the others. For the common forms use line-chart, area-chart, bar-chart, donut-chart, sparkline, heatmap or radial-progress directly.
meta.example:
<ChartContainer aspect={2} table={{ caption: "Signups", columns: ["Day", "Signups"], rows: [["Mon", 4], ["Tue", 9]] }}>
  {({ width, height }) => (
    <ChartSvg label="Signups by day" width={width} height={height}>
      <rect x={0} y={height - 40} width={width / 3} height={40} className={chartSeries(0).fill} />
      <rect x={width / 2} y={height - 90} width={width / 3} height={90} className={chartSeries(0).fill} />
    </ChartSvg>
  )}
</ChartContainer>
<ChartLegend items={[{ label: "Signups", index: 0 }]} mark="rect" />

items.name: circle-pack
items.title: Circle Pack
items.description: A hierarchy as circles inside circles: each group an outline holding its parts, each part a circle whose area is its size, with zooming into a group by click or Enter and back out by the trail or Backspace.

meta.when: Showing groups and their members when the grouping matters more than precise sizes: topics and their articles, teams and their projects. To compare sizes closely use treemap or bar-chart; for levels as rings use sunburst.
meta.example:
<CirclePack
  label="Articles by topic"
  data={{
    name: "All articles",
    children: [
      { name: "Science", children: [{ name: "Space", value: 40 }, { name: "Biology", value: 25 }] },
      { name: "Arts", children: [{ name: "Film", value: 30 }, { name: "Music", value: 18 }] },
    ],
  }}
/>

items.name: density-chart
items.title: Density Chart
items.description: Where many points crowd together, drawn as filled contour bands of one hue from faint to strong (like the lines of a height map), with the points optionally on top and each point reachable by arrow keys.

meta.when: Two measures over hundreds or thousands of points, where a scatter-chart would be a blot: where the bulk lies, whether there are two clusters. For under a few hundred points use scatter-chart; for one measure's spread use histogram.
meta.example:
<DensityChart
  label="Trip length against fare"
  data={[{ km: 2, fare: 8 }, { km: 3, fare: 10 }, { km: 2.5, fare: 9 }, { km: 12, fare: 31 }, { km: 11, fare: 29 }]}
  x="km"
  y="fare"
  xLabel="Distance (km)"
  yLabel="Fare"
  showPoints
/>

items.name: donut-chart
items.title: Donut Chart
items.description: A ring showing how one whole splits into at most five parts, with a label in the centre and each part's value and share in the legend.

meta.when: Parts of a whole at a glance, when there are few parts and they differ clearly. To compare parts that are close in size, or more than five, use bar-chart with `orientation="horizontal"`; for one ratio against a limit use radial-progress.
meta.example:
<DonutChart
  label="Traffic by source"
  data={[
    { source: "Search", visits: 5200 },
    { source: "Direct", visits: 3100 },
    { source: "Referral", visits: 1400 },
  ]}
  name="source"
  value="visits"
  centerLabel="Visits"
/>

items.name: fan-chart
items.title: Fan Chart
items.description: A forecast drawn honestly: what was observed as a solid line, then the median forecast with nested bands for its intervals (90 %, 50 % …) that widen as the forecast reaches further, with arrow-key reading of every point.

meta.when: Showing a prediction or an estimate with its uncertainty: a forecast, a model's range, a confidence band around a trend. For a series with no uncertainty use line-chart; for the spread of measured values use box-plot.
meta.example:
<FanChart
  label="Visitors, observed and forecast"
  data={[
    { week: 1, observed: 120 },
    { week: 2, observed: 132 },
    { week: 3, observed: 128, median: 128, low90: 128, high90: 128, low50: 128, high50: 128 },
    { week: 4, median: 136, low90: 118, high90: 152, low50: 128, high50: 143 },
    { week: 5, median: 141, low90: 110, high90: 170, low50: 126, high50: 155 },
  ]}
  x="week"
  observed="observed"
  median="median"
  intervals={[
    { low: "low90", high: "high90", label: "90% interval" },
    { low: "low50", high: "high50", label: "50% interval" },
  ]}
  forecastFrom={3}
  labels={{ observed: "Observed", median: "Forecast (median)", forecast: "Forecast" }}
/>

items.name: gantt-chart
items.title: Gantt Chart
items.description: Tasks as bars along a time axis, one row each, under optional group headings: how far each has got, which must finish before another starts (arrows), milestones as diamonds and a line for today, with Up and Down reading each task.

meta.when: Planning or reporting work over time: a project plan, a release schedule, a timeline of events with lengths. For events without length use timeline (a list) or a line-chart annotation; for a calendar of single days use calendar or calendar-heatmap.
meta.example:
<GanttChart
  label="Launch plan"
  tasks={[
    { id: "design", label: "Design", start: "2026-03-02", end: "2026-03-13", group: "Product", progress: 1 },
    { id: "build", label: "Build", start: "2026-03-09", end: "2026-04-03", group: "Product", progress: 0.4, dependsOn: ["design"] },
    { id: "launch", label: "Launch", start: "2026-04-06", end: "2026-04-06", group: "Marketing", milestone: true, dependsOn: ["build"] },
  ]}
  today="2026-03-20"
/>

items.name: heatmap
items.title: Heatmap
items.description: A matrix of cells (day by hour, for example) coloured on one-hue scale from faint to the highlight colour, with a tooltip, arrow-key reading and a scale legend.

meta.when: Spotting patterns across two categories at once: when it is busy, which pairs stand out. To compare exact amounts use bar-chart; for one row of values over time use line-chart.
meta.example:
<Heatmap
  label="Sessions by day and hour"
  data={[
    { day: "Mon", hour: "09", sessions: 12 },
    { day: "Mon", hour: "10", sessions: 30 },
    { day: "Tue", hour: "09", sessions: 8 },
    { day: "Tue", hour: "10", sessions: 21 },
  ]}
  x="hour"
  y="day"
  value="sessions"
/>

items.name: histogram
items.title: Histogram
items.description: How the values of one measure are spread: the range cut into equal bins, each bar as tall as the number of values that fall in it, with arrow-key reading of each bin.

meta.when: Seeing the shape of a distribution: where most values are, how wide, whether there are two humps or a long tail. To compare the spread of several groups use box-plot; to compare totals across categories use bar-chart.
meta.example:
<Histogram
  label="Delivery times"
  data={[{ minutes: 22 }, { minutes: 31 }, { minutes: 28 }, { minutes: 45 }, { minutes: 26 }, { minutes: 33 }]}
  value="minutes"
  valueLabel="Minutes"
  bins={8}
/>

items.name: line-chart
items.title: Line Chart
items.description: A line chart of one or more series over a numeric or time x, with a crosshair tooltip, arrow-key reading and labels at the line ends.

meta.when: Change over time or along a number, for up to about five series on one shared scale. For a single series whose volume matters use area-chart; for separate categories use bar-chart; never plot two different units against two y axes, use two charts.
meta.example:
<LineChart
  label="Requests and errors per day"
  data={[
    { day: new Date("2026-03-01"), requests: 120, errors: 4 },
    { day: new Date("2026-03-02"), requests: 180, errors: 9 },
    { day: new Date("2026-03-03"), requests: 150, errors: 3 },
  ]}
  x="day"
  series={[
    { key: "requests", label: "Requests" },
    { key: "errors", label: "Errors" },
  ]}
/>

items.name: network-graph
items.title: Network Graph
items.description: Things and the links between them, placed by a force layout that is run to rest before it is drawn (so it is the same every time and never moves on its own), with each node's links lit on hover or focus and every node reachable by arrow keys.

meta.when: Showing who or what is connected to what: clusters, bridges between groups, the most linked items. Keep it to a few hundred nodes. For amounts flowing in one direction use sankey-chart; for a hierarchy use treemap or tree-view; for a process the person edits use flow-diagram.
meta.example:
<NetworkGraph
  label="Libraries and what they use"
  nodes={[{ id: "app", group: "Apps" }, { id: "ui", group: "Libraries" }, { id: "charts", group: "Libraries" }, { id: "maths", group: "Libraries" }]}
  links={[{ source: "app", target: "ui" }, { source: "app", target: "charts" }, { source: "charts", target: "maths" }]}
/>

items.name: radial-progress
items.title: Radial Progress
items.description: A ring gauge for one value against a limit, with the value and a label in the centre.

meta.when: One ratio: a quota used, a score, a goal reached. Size it with a width class (`w-32` by default). For several ratios side by side use a list of bars (bar-chart horizontal), not a ring each; for parts of a whole use donut-chart.
meta.example:
<RadialProgress value={72} label="Storage used" />
<RadialProgress value={3} max={5} label="Steps done" formatValue={(value) => `${value} of 5`} className="w-40" />

items.name: sankey-chart
items.title: Sankey Chart
items.description: Flows between stages as bands whose widths are the amounts: where a total comes from, where it goes and what is lost on the way, with every node and band reachable by arrow keys.

meta.when: Showing how amounts move through steps or between categories: a budget from sources to uses, visitors through a sign-up, energy from fuel to use. For a single funnel of shrinking steps use funnel-chart; for links without amounts use network-graph; for two-way flows between the same groups use chord-diagram.
meta.example:
<SankeyChart
  label="Where the money goes"
  nodes={[{ id: "income", label: "Income" }, { id: "rent", label: "Rent" }, { id: "food", label: "Food" }, { id: "saved", label: "Saved" }]}
  links={[
    { source: "income", target: "rent", value: 1200 },
    { source: "income", target: "food", value: 500 },
    { source: "income", target: "saved", value: 300 },
  ]}
/>

items.name: scatter-chart
items.title: Scatter Chart
items.description: Points placed by two numbers, optionally sized by a third (a bubble chart) and grouped by a category, with the nearest point read under the pointer and every point reachable by arrow keys.

meta.when: Showing how two measures relate across many things: does one rise with the other, which stand apart. Give `size` for a third measure as bubble area. For change over time use line-chart; for one measure across categories use bar-chart or dot-plot; for thousands of overlapping points use density-chart.
meta.example:
<ScatterChart
  label="Price against rating"
  data={[
    { name: "Alder", price: 12, rating: 4.1, sold: 320, kind: "Tea" },
    { name: "Birch", price: 18, rating: 4.6, sold: 120, kind: "Tea" },
    { name: "Cedar", price: 9, rating: 3.8, sold: 540, kind: "Coffee" },
  ]}
  x="price"
  y="rating"
  size="sold"
  group="kind"
  name="name"
  xLabel="Price"
  yLabel="Rating"
/>

items.name: small-multiples
items.title: Small Multiples
items.description: The same small chart repeated for each group (a region, a product) in a grid that fits its width, every panel on one shared scale so they can be compared at a glance, each read by arrow keys.

meta.when: Comparing the shape of one measure across many groups, where one chart with many lines would tangle: more than five series, or groups of very different sizes. For up to five series on one chart use line-chart; for one value per group use bar-chart.
meta.example:
<SmallMultiples
  label="Monthly visits by region"
  data={[
    { region: "North", month: 1, visits: 40 }, { region: "North", month: 2, visits: 52 }, { region: "North", month: 3, visits: 61 },
    { region: "South", month: 1, visits: 30 }, { region: "South", month: 2, visits: 28 }, { region: "South", month: 3, visits: 35 },
  ]}
  facet="region"
  x="month"
  y="visits"
  kind="area"
/>

items.name: sparkline
items.title: Sparkline
items.description: A tiny line, area or bar chart with no axes, for a stat tile or a table cell, described in words for assistive technology.

meta.when: The shape of a trend beside a number that carries the value. Size it with classes (`h-8 w-24` by default). When the reader needs to read values off it, use line-chart or bar-chart.
meta.example:
<Sparkline data={[4, 6, 5, 9, 12, 10, 14]} label="Signups, last 7 days" />
<Sparkline data={[3, 8, 2, 7, 5]} type="bar" className="h-6 w-16" />

items.name: sunburst
items.title: Sunburst
items.description: A hierarchy as rings around a centre: each ring a level, each arc a part sized by its share of its parent, with zooming into any arc by click or Enter and back out by the centre, the trail or Backspace.

meta.when: Showing how a total divides level by level when the depth matters as much as the sizes: a path through categories, a file system, a budget in three levels. For sizes that must be compared closely use treemap (areas in rectangles are easier to judge than arcs); for one level use donut-chart.
meta.example:
<Sunburst
  label="Visits by source"
  data={{
    name: "All visits",
    children: [
      { name: "Search", children: [{ name: "Organic", value: 420 }, { name: "Paid", value: 160 }] },
      { name: "Social", children: [{ name: "Video", value: 120 }, { name: "Posts", value: 80 }] },
      { name: "Direct", value: 300 },
    ],
  }}
/>

items.name: treemap
items.title: Treemap
items.description: A whole split into nested rectangles whose areas are the parts' sizes: groups in their own colours, the parts inside them labelled where they fit, with zooming into a group by click or Enter and back out by the trail or Backspace.

meta.when: Showing how a large total divides across a hierarchy (a budget by department and team, storage by folder) when there are too many parts for a donut. For a few parts use donut-chart; to see the levels as rings use sunburst; to compare exact sizes use bar-chart.
meta.example:
<Treemap
  label="Spending by area"
  data={{
    name: "All spending",
    children: [
      { name: "Housing", children: [{ name: "Rent", value: 1200 }, { name: "Power", value: 140 }] },
      { name: "Food", children: [{ name: "Groceries", value: 420 }, { name: "Cafés", value: 90 }] },
      { name: "Travel", value: 260 },
    ],
  }}
/>
